facts.value: Irish was possibly introduced during the Iron Age, began to be written down after Christianisation in the 5th century, and spread to Scotland and the Isle of Man.
Old Irish (6th to 10th century), Middle Irish (10th to 13th century), Early Modern Irish (until the 17th century), Modern Irish (spoken today)
Latin, Old Norse, French, and English
Irish is taught in Irish schools as compulsory but has been criticized for ineffectiveness, with many students showing little evidence of fluency.
There is a growing population of urban Irish speakers, especially in Dublin and Belfast, with the children of such speakers sometimes attending Irish-medium schools.
Traditional rural Irish-speaking areas, known as the Gaeltacht, are in linguistic decline.
English was first introduced during the Norman invasion and became the official language during the Tudor and Cromwellian conquests.
Fewer than 2% of the population of the Republic of Ireland speak Irish on a daily basis.
Under 10% of the population regularly speak Irish, outside of the education system.
English is the de facto official language, but Irish has specific protective measures under the European Charter for Regional or Minority Languages.
Since the 1960s, increased immigration has introduced many more languages from Asia and Eastern Europe.
Other native languages include Shelta, Irish Sign Language, and Northern Ireland Sign Language.
